## How to read this

Each method here starts from something small enough to see all at once, and
each one shows up when the method before it runs out of road.

Every figure comes from real data, drawn by the code above it. Every number in
the text was printed by a cell on this page. If the two ever disagree, believe
the cell.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup — packages, palette, data loaders"
using DataMimic
using DataFrames, Random, Statistics, Printf, LinearAlgebra
using CairoMakie
using Lux, Zygote          # activates the DiffusionGenerator extension

include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "benchmark", "datasets.jl"))

CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png", px_per_unit = 2)

# One restrained palette used consistently: real data is blue throughout,
# synthetic is red, and green marks the thing under discussion.
const REAL   = "#2E5E8C"
const SYNTH  = "#C4553B"
const FOCUS  = "#4F8A6B"
const MUTED  = "#9AA5B1"

set_theme!(theme_minimal();
    fontsize = 13,
    Axis = (; xgridvisible = false, ygridvisible = true,
              ygridcolor = (:black, 0.06),
              topspinevisible = false, rightspinevisible = false,
              leftspinecolor = (:black, 0.25), bottomspinecolor = (:black, 0.25)),
    Legend = (; framevisible = false))

Random.seed!(1234)
nothing
```

# 1. The problem

Let's start with a table you are not allowed to share.

```{julia}
adult = load_adult()
first(adult[:, [:age, :sex, :race, :marital_status, :occupation,
                :hours_per_week, :income]], 6)
```

This is the UCI Adult census extract: about 49,000 people, with age, education,
occupation, marital status, and income. No names, no addresses. Every direct
identifier was stripped out long before it reached us.

And it's still not safe to publish.

### Anonymous does not mean unidentifiable

On its own, each column tells you almost nothing. Plenty of people are 39.
Plenty are married. Plenty work in sales.

Combinations are another matter. So here's the question: as you learn more and
more ordinary facts about someone, how fast do they become the only person in
the file who matches?

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "How many people share your exact combination of attributes? Each bar is the share of the 48,842 records that are unique on that many columns."
# Ordered from coarse to fine, which is what makes the shape visible.
quasi = [:age, :sex, :marital_status, :occupation, :education,
         :native_country, :hours_per_week, :race]

function unique_fraction(df, cols)
    keys_ = collect(zip((df[!, c] for c in cols)...))
    counts = Dict{Any,Int}()
    for k in keys_
        counts[k] = get(counts, k, 0) + 1
    end
    count(k -> counts[k] == 1, keys_) / length(keys_)
end

ks = 1:length(quasi)
fracs = [unique_fraction(adult, quasi[1:k]) for k in ks]

fig = Figure(size = (860, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1];
    xlabel = "number of attributes known", ylabel = "share of people who are unique",
    title = "Re-identification by combination",
    xticks = (ks, string.(ks)))
barplot!(ax, ks, fracs; color = [f > 0.5 ? SYNTH : REAL for f in fracs], width = 0.65)
# The step from 6 to 7 attributes is where a fine-grained column enters.
lines!(ax, [6.5, 6.5], [0, 1.02]; color = FOCUS, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5)
text!(ax, 6.55, 0.95; text = "  + hours_per_week", align = (:left, :center),
      fontsize = 10, color = FOCUS)
for (k, f) in zip(ks, fracs)
    text!(ax, k, f + 0.02; text = @sprintf("%.0f%%", 100f),
          align = (:center, :bottom), fontsize = 10, color = :black)
end
ylims!(ax, 0, 1.08)
hlines!(ax, [0.5]; color = MUTED, linestyle = :dash)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
for k in (4, 6, 7, 8)
    @printf("%d attributes: %5.1f%% of these people are unique in the file\n",
            k, 100 * fracs[k])
end
```

Watch the shape, not any single bar. Four coarse attributes, and almost
everyone is still hidden in a crowd. Six, and three quarters of people are
still safe. Then `hours_per_week` joins the list — ninety-six distinct values
instead of a handful — and the unique share roughly doubles in one step.

That jump is the point. Risk doesn't live in the sensitive columns. It lives in
the fine-grained ones. Nobody would think twice about publishing how many hours
a week someone works, and it does more damage here than anything else, because
it cuts the population into thinner slices.

So publishing this table means publishing these people. Someone who knows seven
ordinary facts about you — the kind on a social media profile — has a coin-flip
chance of finding your row, and then reads off everything else in it.

### So invent new people instead

Synthetic data takes a different route. Instead of blurring or suppressing real
records, you fit a model to the table and draw new rows from it. Nobody in the
output is anybody in particular, because nobody in the output is anybody.

```{julia}
model = fit(CopulaGenerator(), adult; rng = MersenneTwister(1))
syn   = sample(model, nrow(adult); rng = MersenneTwister(2))
first(syn[:, [:age, :sex, :race, :marital_status, :occupation,
              :hours_per_week, :income]], 6)
```

Those rows came out of an estimated distribution. The 39-year-old in row 1 of
the synthetic table has nothing to do with the 39-year-old in row 1 of the real
one.

Which raises the question the rest of this document keeps returning to. Does
that make it safe? And how would you know?

The short answer takes four sections to earn: it helps enormously and
guarantees nothing, until you add something that does.

# 2. What is a column?

Before any model runs, every column is sorted into a kind. Every engine here
reads that decision, and a lot rides on it.

```{julia}
DataFrame(column   = Symbol.(names(adult)),
          kind     = [DataMimic.detect_column_type(adult[!, c]) for c in names(adult)],
          distinct = [length(unique(skipmissing(adult[!, c]))) for c in names(adult)],
          eltype   = [string(nonmissingtype(eltype(adult[!, c]))) for c in names(adult)])
```

Look at `:education_num`. Julia stores it as an integer, but it takes only
sixteen values, and it's really `:education` with numbers attached — a category
in numeric clothing. Now look at `:age`. Also an integer, also whole numbers,
but seventy-four distinct values, and numeric for real: the distance from 30 to
40 means something.

Treat those two columns the same way and you'll be wrong about one of them.

### The rule is cardinality, not storage type

So the decision can't come from the storage type. It comes from a ratio: how
many distinct values does the column hold, against how many rows there are?

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Each numeric column placed by its distinct-value ratio. The ones on the left have few enough levels to be categories."
numcols = [c for c in names(adult) if nonmissingtype(eltype(adult[!, c])) <: Real]
ratios = [length(unique(skipmissing(adult[!, c]))) / nrow(adult) for c in numcols]
kinds  = [DataMimic.detect_column_type(adult[!, c]) for c in numcols]

fig = Figure(size = (860, 320))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10,
    xlabel = "distinct values ÷ rows  (log scale)",
    ylabel = "", title = "Where each numeric column falls",
    yticks = (1:length(numcols), string.(numcols)),
    ygridvisible = false)
scatter!(ax, ratios, 1:length(numcols);
         color = [k === :categorical ? FOCUS : REAL for k in kinds], markersize = 14)
for (i, (r, k)) in enumerate(zip(ratios, kinds))
    text!(ax, r, i; text = "  " * string(k), align = (:left, :center),
          fontsize = 10, color = MUTED)
end
xlims!(ax, minimum(ratios) / 4, maximum(ratios) * 14)
fig
```

### Does getting it wrong actually hurt?

Easy enough to find out. Take one table, force two columns to the wrong kind,
and watch what each engine does about it.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
sub2 = adult[1:8000, [:age, :education_num, :hours_per_week, :workclass,
                      :occupation, :sex, :income]]

function typed_score(gen, hint)
    hints = hint === nothing ? ColumnHint[] : [hint]
    m = fit(gen, sub2; hints = hints, rng = MersenneTwister(3))
    sy = sample(m, nrow(sub2); rng = MersenneTwister(4))
    fidelity_score(sub2, sy).aggregate
end

cases = [("detected correctly",              nothing),
         ("age forced categorical",          ColumnHint(name = :age, kind = :categorical)),
         ("education_num forced continuous", ColumnHint(name = :education_num, kind = :continuous))]

DataFrame(
    typing = first.(cases),
    copula = [typed_score(CopulaGenerator(), h) for (_, h) in cases],
    mst_eps1 = [typed_score(MSTGenerator(ε = 1.0), h) for (_, h) in cases],
)
```

The two engines react very differently. The copula barely notices — one of the
mis-typings even scores a hair better. MST degrades by something like forty
percent.

That split isn't luck. It falls out of how each engine works. The copula models
every column with its empirical distribution, so a column you wrongly called
continuous still gets rebuilt from values that actually occurred. The mistake
is absorbed. MST has no such cushion. It chops everything into contingency
tables, then spends a fixed privacy budget measuring them. Tell it a
seventy-four-level numeric column is a category and it has seventy-four cells
to measure with the same noise, most of them nearly empty.

Which sharpens the advice. The more your engine leans on discretization, and
the tighter your budget, the more a typing mistake costs. On a public copula
fit you can be relaxed about it. On MST at ε = 1 you can't.

### When the rule misfires

There are six kinds: `:continuous`, `:integer`, `:categorical`, `:binary`,
`:constant`, and `:identifier`. The last one is treated differently. An
identifier carries no statistical signal but plenty of disclosure risk, so it
isn't synthesised at all. It's excluded from the model, and unless you give it
a `fill` spec, dropped from the output.

For a customer number, that's right. For this, it's wrong:

```{julia}
german = load_german_credit()
DataFrame(column   = [:credit_amount, :duration_months, :age],
          kind     = [DataMimic.detect_column_type(german[!, c])
                      for c in (:credit_amount, :duration_months, :age)],
          distinct = [length(unique(german[!, c]))
                      for c in (:credit_amount, :duration_months, :age)],
          rows     = fill(nrow(german), 3))
```

`credit_amount` is a loan size in Deutschmarks, about as continuous as a
variable gets. But German Credit has only a thousand rows, and 921 of the loan
amounts are distinct. By ratio alone, that looks exactly like a primary key. So
it's classified as an identifier, excluded, and quietly dropped:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
m_auto = fit(CopulaGenerator(), german; rng = MersenneTwister(11))
s_auto = sample(m_auto, 200; rng = MersenneTwister(12))
setdiff(names(german), names(s_auto))
```

This is the most consequential way column detection goes wrong: the identifier
heuristic misfires on real high-cardinality columns in small datasets. From a
distinct-value ratio alone, "nearly unique" and "is a key" look the same. The
heuristic gets safer as tables get bigger — a continuous column in fifty
thousand rows is rarely 92% distinct.

The fix is to tell it. Every engine here that touches German Credit passes a
hint:

```{julia}
credit_hint = [ColumnHint(name = :credit_amount, kind = :continuous)]
m_hint = fit(CopulaGenerator(), german; hints = credit_hint,
             rng = MersenneTwister(11))
s_hint = sample(m_hint, 200; rng = MersenneTwister(12))
setdiff(names(german), names(s_hint))
```

The lesson isn't about this one column. Detection is a heuristic with a silent
failure mode, so check what it decided. The message it logs is easy to scroll
past in a long fit, and a missing column is easy to miss in a wide table.

# 3. Modelling a table

Now the first real method. The goal is easy to state: estimate a distribution
over rows, well enough to draw new ones from it.

The trouble is that a table is a joint distribution over columns of very
different types — a skewed positive number here, a sixteen-level category
there, a binary flag next to it. Estimating all of that at once is hard.

Copulas get around it by not doing it all at once.

### Sklar's theorem: shape and dependence come apart

The whole method rests on one result. Any joint distribution splits into two
pieces: the marginals — the shape of each column on its own — and a single
function that couples them. Formally, for a joint CDF $F$ with marginals
$F_1, \dots, F_d$ there is a copula $C$ with

$$
F(x_1, \dots, x_d) \;=\; C\bigl(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\bigr),
$$

and $C$ is unique wherever the marginals are continuous.

That split does most of the work. The hard part — every column's individual
shape — stops being a modelling problem: hand each column its own empirical
distribution and you get it back exactly, with no family to choose and no
fitting error. All that's left to estimate is the coupling.

### Step one: strip the shapes away

To get at the coupling, push each column through its own empirical CDF.
Whatever it looked like going in — skewed, bimodal, bounded, spiky — it comes
out uniform on $[0, 1]$. Only the ranks survive.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Two Wine columns before and after the rank transform. The marginal shapes are gone; the dependence is untouched."
wine = load_wine(colour = :white)

pit(v) = (sortperm(sortperm(v)) .- 0.5) ./ length(v)

fig = Figure(size = (900, 720))

ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "residual sugar", ylabel = "count",
           title = "marginal: heavily skewed")
hist!(ax1, wine.residual_sugar; bins = 60, color = (REAL, 0.75), strokewidth = 0)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "F(residual sugar)", ylabel = "count",
           title = "after the transform: uniform")
hist!(ax2, pit(wine.residual_sugar); bins = 60, color = (FOCUS, 0.75), strokewidth = 0)

ax3 = Axis(fig[2, 1]; xlabel = "residual sugar", ylabel = "density",
           title = "joint: shape dominates the picture")
scatter!(ax3, wine.residual_sugar, wine.density;
         color = (REAL, 0.18), markersize = 4)
ylims!(ax3, 0.985, 1.005)

ax4 = Axis(fig[2, 2]; xlabel = "F(residual sugar)", ylabel = "F(density)",
           title = "joint: pure dependence")
scatter!(ax4, pit(wine.residual_sugar), pit(wine.density);
         color = (FOCUS, 0.18), markersize = 4)
fig
```

The bottom-right panel is the whole remaining problem. Both axes are uniform by
construction, so nothing about the original shapes is left. Any structure you
can still see there is dependence and nothing else.

### Step two: sample, then put the shapes back on

Sampling is the same trip in reverse. Draw a point from the fitted copula, then
push each coordinate back through the matching inverse CDF. The marginals come
back exactly right — by construction, not by approximation — which is why
copula output looks so plausible column by column.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Real against synthetic on the same axes. The dependence structure survives the round trip."
wine_model = fit(CopulaGenerator(), wine; rng = MersenneTwister(5))
wine_syn   = sample(wine_model, nrow(wine); rng = MersenneTwister(6))

fig = Figure(size = (900, 360))
for (j, (df, ttl, col)) in enumerate(((wine, "real", REAL),
                                      (wine_syn, "synthetic", SYNTH)))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; xlabel = "alcohol", ylabel = j == 1 ? "density" : "",
              title = ttl)
    scatter!(ax, df.alcohol, df.density; color = (col, 0.18), markersize = 4)
    ylims!(ax, 0.985, 1.005); xlims!(ax, 7.5, 15)
end
fig
```

### Does the whole dependence structure survive?

One scatter plot is an anecdote. Look at every pair of columns at once.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Spearman correlation across all eleven Wine columns. The third panel is the error, on a five-times tighter colour scale."
wine_cols = Symbol.(names(wine))
short(c) = (s = string(c); length(s) <= 9 ? s : s[1:8] * ".")
labels = short.(wine_cols)

spearman(df) = cor(hcat([pit(Float64.(df[!, c])) for c in wine_cols]...))
Cr, Cs = spearman(wine), spearman(wine_syn)

function corr_panel(pos, M, ttl, lims; ylabels)
    ax = Axis(pos; title = ttl, aspect = 1,
        xticks = (1:length(labels), labels),
        yticks = (1:length(labels), ylabels ? labels : fill("", length(labels))),
        xticklabelrotation = π/2, xticklabelsize = 8, yticklabelsize = 8,
        ygridvisible = false)
    heatmap!(ax, M; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = lims)
end

fig = Figure(size = (1000, 400))
corr_panel(fig[1, 1], Cr, "real", (-1, 1); ylabels = true)
corr_panel(fig[1, 2], Cs, "synthetic", (-1, 1); ylabels = false)
Colorbar(fig[1, 3]; colormap = :RdBu, limits = (-1, 1), width = 9, label = "ρ")
hm = corr_panel(fig[1, 4], Cs .- Cr, "error (5× tighter scale)", (-0.2, 0.2);
                ylabels = false)
Colorbar(fig[1, 5], hm; width = 9, label = "Δρ")
colgap!(fig.layout, 6)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
@printf("largest correlation error: %.3f    mean: %.3f\n",
        maximum(abs.(Cs .- Cr)), mean(abs.(Cs .- Cr)))
```

### Categorical columns need one more idea

There's a problem hiding in step one. A copula wants continuous marginals, and
a category doesn't have one. Its CDF is a staircase, so every "Married" in the
file lands on the same single point instead of spreading across an interval.
The uniformity we relied on is gone.

The repair is small. A level occupies the CDF interval $[F(k-1), F(k)]$, so
rather than mapping it to the top of its step, map it to a uniform draw
somewhere inside that step. This is the **distributional transform**. Sampling
inverts the same staircase to get the level back.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "A categorical CDF is a staircase (left). The distributional transform spreads each level across its own step (right), which is what makes it usable as a copula coordinate."
levels_ = sort(unique(skipmissing(adult.education)))
probs = [count(==(l), skipmissing(adult.education)) for l in levels_]
probs = probs ./ sum(probs)
cdf = cumsum(probs)

fig = Figure(size = (960, 380))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; title = "empirical CDF of a 16-level column",
    xlabel = "level (ordered by index)", ylabel = "F", ygridvisible = true)
stairs!(ax1, 0:length(levels_), vcat(0.0, cdf); color = REAL, linewidth = 2.5,
        step = :post)
for (k, c) in enumerate(cdf)
    lines!(ax1, [k - 1, k], [c, c]; color = (REAL, 0.35), linewidth = 6)
end

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; title = "each level spread across its own step",
    xlabel = "uniform draw inside [F(k-1), F(k)]", ylabel = "count")
rng = MersenneTwister(9)
u = Float64[]
for (k, l) in enumerate(levels_)
    lo = k == 1 ? 0.0 : cdf[k-1]
    n = count(==(l), skipmissing(adult.education))
    append!(u, lo .+ rand(rng, n) .* (cdf[k] - lo))
end
hist!(ax2, u; bins = 80, color = (FOCUS, 0.8), strokewidth = 0)
vlines!(ax2, cdf[1:end-1]; color = MUTED, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 0.8)
fig
```

The right panel is uniform again, which is what the copula needed. Dependence
between a categorical column and a numeric one now gets modelled instead of
thrown away.

Two consequences follow, and between them they explain why the package ships
two copula families.

First, the association this can express is monotone in the level ordering. For
a nominal variable that ordering is arbitrary — `occupation` has no natural
sequence, we just sorted it somehow. So we capture part of the dependence, not
all of it.

Second, a Gaussian copula has only a correlation matrix to work with, so
monotone dependence is all it can express. The nonparametric Beta copula can
represent the lumpy, non-monotone structure an arbitrary ordering produces,
which is why it's the default.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
sub = adult[1:8000, [:age, :education, :occupation, :hours_per_week, :sex, :income]]
holdout = adult[8001:14000, names(sub)]

function copula_utility(kind)
    m = fit(CopulaGenerator(kind), sub; rng = MersenneTwister(7))
    s = sample(m, nrow(sub); rng = MersenneTwister(8))
    utility_tstr(sub, s, :income; test = holdout, rng = MersenneTwister(10))
end

b, g = copula_utility(:beta), copula_utility(:gaussian)
DataFrame(copula = ["beta (default)", "gaussian"],
          f1_from_synthetic = [b.synth_score, g.synth_score],
          f1_from_real      = [b.real_score,  g.real_score],
          ratio             = [b.ratio,       g.ratio])
```

On a mixed table the gap is large, which is why `:beta` is the default. Reach
for `:gaussian` when you want a Gaussian dependence structure specifically —
not when you want a faster one.

### What a copula cannot do

Three blind spots.

- **Dependence is pairwise.** A three-way interaction — a relationship between
  A and B that reverses depending on C — is not represented.
- **Nominal ordering is arbitrary**, as above.
- **A single-level column** can't be encoded at all, so it's left out of the
  copula and drawn independently.

These are what the diffusion model in section 8 exists to escape. We'll get
there. There's a more urgent question first.

# 4. Can I publish this?

Section 3 gave us a synthetic table. Every row was generated; not one is a copy
of a real person. The natural conclusion is that it's safe to release.

Let's try to break it.

### The attack

Here's the question an attacker wants answered: *was Alice in the training
data?* They know Alice's age, occupation, education, hours worked — ordinary
facts about a person. They have the published synthetic table. That's all they
get.

The attack is one line of intuition. A model fitted to data containing Alice
will lean, slightly, toward producing rows that look like Alice. So measure how
close Alice's record sits to its nearest synthetic neighbour, and if that
distance is small, guess "member".

To test it we need ground truth, so we fit on half the records and hold the
other half back. The attacker's only score is distance to the nearest synthetic
row, and the question is how well it separates the two halves.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — Gower distance, nearest-neighbour scores, AUC"
mia_cols = [:age, :education_num, :hours_per_week, :capital_gain,
            :workclass, :education, :marital_status, :occupation, :sex, :income]
full = dropmissing(adult[:, mia_cols])
mia_num = [:age, :education_num, :hours_per_week, :capital_gain]
mia_cat = [:workclass, :education, :marital_status, :occupation, :sex, :income]

# Mixed-type distance: numeric scaled to its range, categorical 0/1 mismatch.
function encode(df, scales)
    N = Matrix{Float64}(undef, nrow(df), length(mia_num))
    for (j, c) in enumerate(mia_num)
        N[:, j] = Float64.(df[!, c]) ./ scales[j]
    end
    C = Matrix{String}(undef, nrow(df), length(mia_cat))
    for (j, c) in enumerate(mia_cat)
        C[:, j] = string.(df[!, c])
    end
    (N, C)
end

function nearest_distance(Q, S)
    (QN, QC), (SN, SC) = Q, S
    out = Vector{Float64}(undef, size(QN, 1))
    for i in axes(QN, 1)
        best = Inf
        for k in axes(SN, 1)
            d = 0.0
            @inbounds for j in axes(QN, 2); d += abs(QN[i, j] - SN[k, j]); end
            @inbounds for j in axes(QC, 2); d += QC[i, j] == SC[k, j] ? 0.0 : 1.0; end
            d < best && (best = d)
        end
        out[i] = best
    end
    out
end

# Area under the ROC curve, computed from ranks. Closer ⇒ guessed "member".
function attack_auc(d_member, d_nonmember)
    ranks = sortperm(sortperm(vcat(d_member, d_nonmember)))
    n1, n2 = length(d_member), length(d_nonmember)
    u = sum(ranks[1:n1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2
    1 - u / (n1 * n2)
end

function run_attack(n; q = 400, seed = 20)
    perm = randperm(MersenneTwister(seed), nrow(full))
    members    = full[perm[1:n], :]
    nonmembers = full[perm[n+1:n+min(n, nrow(full) - n)], :]

    m   = fit(CopulaGenerator(), members; rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 1))
    syn = sample(m, n; rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 2))

    scales = [max(maximum(Float64.(members[!, c])) -
                  minimum(Float64.(members[!, c])), 1.0) for c in mia_num]
    S  = encode(syn, scales)
    qq = min(q, nrow(members), nrow(nonmembers))
    dm = nearest_distance(encode(members[1:qq, :], scales), S)
    dn = nearest_distance(encode(nonmembers[1:qq, :], scales), S)
    (; n, auc = attack_auc(dm, dn), dm, dn)
end

attacks = [run_attack(n) for n in (500, 2_000, 10_000, 40_000)]
DataFrame(rows_fitted = [a.n for a in attacks],
          attack_auc  = [a.auc for a in attacks],
          median_member    = [median(a.dm) for a in attacks],
          median_nonmember = [median(a.dn) for a in attacks])
```

An AUC of 0.5 would mean the attack is no better than a coin flip. That's not
what we're looking at.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Left: how close each real record sits to its nearest synthetic neighbour, for a model fitted to 10,000 rows. Right: the attack's accuracy against the size of the training set."
a = attacks[3]

fig = Figure(size = (960, 380))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "distance to nearest synthetic record",
    ylabel = "density", title = "fitted on 10,000 rows")
hist!(ax1, a.dm; bins = 40, normalization = :pdf,
      color = (SYNTH, 0.6), label = "in the training data")
hist!(ax1, a.dn; bins = 40, normalization = :pdf,
      color = (REAL, 0.5), label = "held out")
xlims!(ax1, 0, quantile(vcat(a.dm, a.dn), 0.97))
axislegend(ax1; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "rows used to fit the model",
    ylabel = "attack AUC", title = "more data does not fix it",
    xticks = ([a.n for a in attacks], string.([a.n for a in attacks])))
lines!(ax2, [a.n for a in attacks], [a.auc for a in attacks];
       color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2.5)
scatter!(ax2, [a.n for a in attacks], [a.auc for a in attacks];
         color = SYNTH, markersize = 10)
hlines!(ax2, [0.5]; color = MUTED, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax2, first([a.n for a in attacks]), 0.52; text = "guessing",
      align = (:left, :bottom), fontsize = 10, color = MUTED)
ylims!(ax2, 0.45, 0.85)
fig
```

Two things come out of those panels, and the second is the uncomfortable one.

The distributions separate. Records that were in the training data sit
measurably closer to the synthetic output than records that were held out.

And it doesn't get better with more data. There's a comforting intuition that a
model fitted to forty thousand people can't be memorising any one of them —
too much averaging. The right-hand panel says otherwise. The attack works about
as well at forty thousand rows as at five hundred.

### Why the copula leaks

The mechanism isn't subtle. It falls straight out of the design from section 3.

The copula models each column with its empirical distribution. That's what made
the marginals come back exactly right. But an empirical distribution *is* the
training values. The set of ages this model can emit is the set of ages it saw,
and sampling interpolates between observed values rather than inventing new
ones.

So the synthetic table is built from real people's values, shuffled and
recombined. Nobody's whole row survives, which is why nothing matches exactly.
But enough of each person survives, spread across columns, for a
nearest-neighbour query to find them.

The point reaches well past this package. A model that reproduces your data
well has, by construction, kept information about it. Fidelity and privacy
pull against each other, and no amount of care in the modelling gets you out
of it.

### What would fix it?

Not a better distance metric. Not more rows. Not a different copula family.

The missing piece is a bound. Nothing here limits how much one record can
influence the output. All we have is the observation that it seems to be a lot,
and an observation is not a guarantee — the next attacker may be cleverer than
the one we just wrote.

What we want is a method whose output provably barely depends on whether any
one person was in the input. That's the next section.

# 5. Differential privacy

Here's the guarantee we want, in plain language: **if I remove you from the
dataset, the output should look essentially the same.**

If that holds, no attacker can work out whether you were in the data — however
clever, however well-informed, however many other databases they hold —
because the output barely depends on the answer. There's nothing to detect.

### The smallest possible example

Forget tables for a minute. Say I want to survey how many people have done
something they'd rather not admit to, and I want an honest answer.

Here's a protocol that gets one. Every respondent flips a coin in private,
where I can't see it.

- **Heads** — answer truthfully.
- **Tails** — flip again, and answer "yes" on heads, "no" on tails.

Now nobody can be held to their answer. A "yes" might be true, or it might be a
coin. That's plausible deniability, and it's built into the mechanism rather
than promised by the person collecting the data. You don't have to trust me.
You have to trust the coin.

And the aggregate survives anyway.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Randomized response. Each individual answer is deniable, yet the population proportion is recoverable — and the estimate tightens as the sample grows."
function randomized_response(truth::AbstractVector{Bool}, rng)
    [rand(rng) < 0.5 ? t : rand(rng) < 0.5 for t in truth]
end

# Half the answers are noise with mean 1/2, so:  observed = p/2 + 1/4
recover(observed_rate) = 2 * observed_rate - 0.5

true_p = 0.30
rng = MersenneTwister(77)
sizes = round.(Int, exp10.(range(2, 5; length = 22)))
ests = [recover(mean(randomized_response(rand(rng, n) .< true_p, rng))) for n in sizes]

fig = Figure(size = (960, 360))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "what one person reports", ylabel = "",
    title = "an individual answer says almost nothing",
    yticks = ([1, 2], ["truth = no", "truth = yes"]), ygridvisible = false)
for (row, p_yes) in ((1, 0.25), (2, 0.75))
    barplot!(ax1, [row - 0.0], [p_yes]; direction = :x, width = 0.45,
             color = (SYNTH, 0.85))
    barplot!(ax1, [row - 0.0], [1 - p_yes]; direction = :x, width = 0.45,
             color = (REAL, 0.35), offset = p_yes)
    text!(ax1, p_yes / 2, row; text = @sprintf("says yes %.0f%%", 100p_yes),
          align = (:center, :center), fontsize = 10, color = :white)
end
xlims!(ax1, 0, 1)
ax1.xlabel = "probability"

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "respondents",
    ylabel = "estimated proportion", title = "the aggregate is recoverable")
hlines!(ax2, [true_p]; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2, label = "truth = 0.30")
scatter!(ax2, sizes, ests; color = SYNTH, markersize = 7)
lines!(ax2, sizes, ests; color = (SYNTH, 0.4))
axislegend(ax2; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)
ylims!(ax2, 0, 0.6)
fig
```

Someone who reports "yes" is only three times likelier to have meant it than
not. That ratio — how much more probable your true answer makes the observed
one — is the whole idea. Differential privacy is that ratio, bounded and given
a name.

### The definition, now that it's obvious

A mechanism $M$ is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differentially private if, for any
two datasets $D$ and $D'$ differing in a single record, and any set of outputs
$S$:

$$
\Pr[M(D) \in S] \;\le\; e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] \;+\; \delta .
$$

Read it as: removing one person changes the probability of any outcome by at
most a factor of $e^{\varepsilon}$. The coin-flip protocol satisfies this with
$\varepsilon = \ln 3 \approx 1.1$ — the three from a moment ago, inside a
logarithm.

The $\delta$ term is an escape hatch: a small probability that the bound just
fails. It has to stay well below $1/n$. At $\delta \approx 1/n$, a mechanism is
allowed to publish somebody's whole record now and then and still call itself
private. DataMimic defaults it to `1e-5`.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "What ε permits. The shaded band is the range of output probabilities compatible with the guarantee once one record changes — narrow at small ε, effectively unconstrained by ε = 10."
eps_grid = range(0.01, 5; length = 300)
base = 0.30

fig = Figure(size = (860, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "ε", ylabel = "probability of the same outcome",
    title = "how much can one person change the answer?")
band!(ax, eps_grid, base .* exp.(-eps_grid), min.(base .* exp.(eps_grid), 1.0);
      color = (SYNTH, 0.18))
lines!(ax, eps_grid, min.(base .* exp.(eps_grid), 1.0); color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2)
lines!(ax, eps_grid, base .* exp.(-eps_grid); color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2)
hlines!(ax, [base]; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash,
        label = "without you: 0.30")
for (e, lbl) in ((0.5, "strict"), (1.0, "common"), (3.0, "weak"))
    vlines!(ax, [e]; color = MUTED, linewidth = 0.8)
    text!(ax, e, 0.96; text = "  " * lbl, align = (:left, :top),
          fontsize = 10, color = MUTED)
end
axislegend(ax; position = :lt, labelsize = 10)
ylims!(ax, 0, 1)
fig
```

At $\varepsilon = 0.5$, your presence in the data can move any probability by
at most about 65% in relative terms. At $\varepsilon = 3$ it can move it
twentyfold, which is barely a promise. So "differentially private" with no
number attached tells you almost nothing.

### Three properties that make it usable

Three facts turn that definition into something you can build a library on.

**Sensitivity sets the noise.** To release a statistic privately, add noise
scaled to how much one record could change it. A count moves by at most 1 when
a person comes or goes, so counts are cheap. A sum of unbounded values could
move by anything, so it has to be clipped first. Every mechanism in this
package is a version of that pattern.

**Composition adds up, so ε is a budget.** Ask two private questions and the
privacy loss accumulates. This is the part that catches people out:
$\varepsilon$ is not a per-query setting, it's a total, divided across
everything the algorithm does — every marginal, every covariance, every choice.
DataMimic composes under zero-concentrated DP (zCDP), which is tighter than
adding naively across many mechanisms.

**Post-processing is free.** Anything computed from a private output stays
private, at no further cost. That's not a technicality; it's the reason
synthetic data works at all. Once the model is private you can draw a thousand
rows from it, or a million, without spending anything more, and everything
downstream inherits the guarantee.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "How each engine divides a single budget across the steps it must take. Nothing here is free except the reconciliation and the sampling."
splits = [
    ("MSTGenerator", ["select tree" => 0.30, "1-way marginals" => 0.20,
                      "2-way marginals" => 0.50]),
    ("DPCopulaGenerator", ["histogram marginals" => 0.50,
                           "private covariance" => 0.50]),
]
fig = Figure(size = (880, 260))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "share of the total ε budget", ylabel = "",
    yticks = (1:length(splits), first.(splits)), ygridvisible = false,
    title = "Where the budget goes")
palette = [REAL, FOCUS, SYNTH]
for (row, (_, parts)) in enumerate(splits)
    off = 0.0
    for (k, (label, frac)) in enumerate(parts)
        barplot!(ax, [row], [frac]; direction = :x, width = 0.5,
                 offset = off, color = (palette[k], 0.85))
        text!(ax, off + frac / 2, row; text = label, align = (:center, :center),
              fontsize = 10, color = :white)
        off += frac
    end
end
xlims!(ax, 0, 1)
fig
```

### What it costs

None of this is free. The noise that buys the guarantee also degrades the
output, and the only way to learn what it costs on your data is to measure it.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The privacy–utility curve on German Credit. Steep at the left, flat at the right — the useful question is where your data stops improving."
eps_grid2 = [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]

sweep = privacy_utility_sweep(MSTGenerator, german, eps_grid2,
            (r, s) -> fidelity_score(r, s).aggregate;
            hints = credit_hint, rng = MersenneTwister(31))
vals = [r.metric_result for r in sweep]

public = let m = fit(CopulaGenerator(), german; hints = credit_hint,
                    rng = MersenneTwister(32))
    fidelity_score(german, sample(m, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(33))).aggregate
end

fig = Figure(size = (860, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "ε  (log scale)",
    ylabel = "fidelity distance  (lower is better)",
    title = "what a privacy budget costs",
    xticks = (eps_grid2, string.(eps_grid2)))
lines!(ax, eps_grid2, vals; color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2.5)
scatter!(ax, eps_grid2, vals; color = SYNTH, markersize = 9)
hlines!(ax, [public]; color = REAL, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2,
        label = "no privacy at all")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

The gap between the curve and the dashed line is the price of the guarantee. It
narrows as ε grows, as you'd expect. It also narrows as the dataset grows,
which is less obvious and matters more: sensitivity fixes the noise regardless
of how many rows you have, while the signal keeps getting stronger.

The next three sections are variations on one question — given a budget, how
should an engine spend it?

# 6. Private copulas

The copula from section 3 came in two halves: the marginals and the dependence.
Making it private means making both halves private, and the two halves want
different mechanisms.

### Private marginals

A marginal is a histogram — a set of counts. Counts are the easiest thing in
differential privacy: add or remove one person and a count moves by exactly
one. Sensitivity 1, so the noise is cheap.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The same histogram released at three budgets. Noise is added to every bin, so small bins are the ones that suffer."
counts = [count(==(l), skipmissing(adult.workclass))
          for l in sort(unique(skipmissing(adult.workclass)))]
labs = sort(unique(skipmissing(adult.workclass)))

fig = Figure(size = (980, 330))
for (j, eps) in enumerate((0.1, 1.0, Inf))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j];
        title = isinf(eps) ? "no noise" : "ε = $eps",
        xticks = (1:length(labs), string.(labs)),
        xticklabelrotation = π/4, xticklabelsize = 8,
        ylabel = j == 1 ? "count" : "")
    noisy = isinf(eps) ? counts :
            counts .+ randn(MersenneTwister(40 + j), length(counts)) .* (2 / eps)
    barplot!(ax, 1:length(labs), max.(noisy, 0);
             color = isinf(eps) ? (REAL, 0.85) : (SYNTH, 0.85))
    hlines!(ax, [0]; color = MUTED, linewidth = 0.8)
end
fig
```

The noise lands unevenly. Large categories barely feel it — a few dozen either
way on a count of thirty thousand is nothing. Small ones are wrecked, and some
go negative before being clamped back to zero.

That asymmetry is the general shape of differential privacy on real data: it
taxes the rare far more heavily than the common. Which is fair enough, since
being rare is what makes a person identifiable. It also means the minority
groups in your data lose the most fidelity. Know that before you publish.

### Private dependence: Analyze-Gauss

The other half of the copula is a covariance matrix. The standard way to
release one privately is **Analyze-Gauss** (Dwork, Talwar, Thakurta & Zhang,
2014): clip the rows so no single one can dominate, form the second-moment
matrix, add Gaussian noise.

One detail is easy to get wrong, and getting it wrong silently halves your
protection. A covariance matrix is symmetric, so the noise has to be symmetric
too — draw the upper triangle and mirror it across the diagonal. Draw both
triangles independently and every off-diagonal entry gets half the intended
variance, at which point the ε you advertise is not the ε you have.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Wine's correlation structure at three budgets. The strong relationships survive; the weak ones dissolve into noise first."
wnum = Matrix{Float64}(wine[:, Symbol.(names(wine))])
C0 = cor(wnum)

fig = Figure(size = (1000, 300))
for (j, eps) in enumerate((0.5, 2.0, Inf))
    M = if isinf(eps)
        C0
    else
        r = MersenneTwister(50 + j)
        E = randn(r, size(C0)...) .* (0.35 / eps)
        E = (E .+ E') ./ 2                    # symmetric noise, as above
        clamp.(C0 .+ E, -1, 1)
    end
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; aspect = 1,
        title = isinf(eps) ? "no noise" : "ε = $eps",
        xticksvisible = false, yticksvisible = false,
        xticklabelsvisible = false, yticklabelsvisible = false,
        ygridvisible = false)
    heatmap!(ax, M; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = (-1, 1))
end
Colorbar(fig[1, 4]; colormap = :RdBu, limits = (-1, 1), width = 9, label = "ρ")
fig
```

Put the two halves back together and you have `DPCopulaGenerator`: private
histograms for the marginals, a private covariance for the coupling, and the
budget split evenly between them.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
dpc = fit(DPCopulaGenerator(ε = 1.0), wine; rng = MersenneTwister(51))
dpc_syn = sample(dpc, nrow(wine); rng = MersenneTwister(52))

DataFrame(engine = ["CopulaGenerator (no guarantee)", "DPCopulaGenerator (ε = 1)"],
          fidelity = [fidelity_score(wine, wine_syn).aggregate,
                      fidelity_score(wine, dpc_syn).aggregate])
```

This is the engine for continuous-heavy data, and Wine is that shape. A
covariance matrix is a natural summary of eleven correlated measurements. It is
a poor summary of nine unordered categories, which is what the next section is
for.

# 7. MST: privacy for discrete data

MST won the NIST differential privacy synthetic data challenge. Its central
idea is about budgeting: you can't afford to measure everything, so spend what
you have on the relationships that matter most.

Count the marginals. A table with $d$ columns has $d$ one-way marginals and
$\binom{d}{2}$ two-way ones. Measure all of them privately and the budget
splits so many ways that each measurement drowns in noise. Measure none of the
two-way ones and every relationship in the table is gone.

MST takes the middle road: measure a chosen few.

### The six steps

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
# credit_amount needs the hint from section 2, or it is treated as an
# identifier and dropped.
mst_model = fit(MSTGenerator(ε = 1.0, δ = 1e-5), german; hints = credit_hint,
                rng = MersenneTwister(60))
mst_syn = sample(mst_model, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(61))
first(mst_syn[:, [:checking_status, :duration_months, :purpose,
                  :credit_amount, :age, :credit_risk]], 5)
```

1. **Discretize.** Everything becomes bins — numeric columns into 32
   equal-width bins by default — because the algorithm works over contingency
   tables. This is why column typing mattered so much in section 2.
2. **Measure every one-way marginal** under Gaussian noise. There are only $d$
   of them, so they're cheap, and they anchor each column's distribution.
3. **Choose a spanning tree.** Score each candidate pair by how badly the
   independence assumption fails for it, then pick a maximum spanning tree over
   columns using the **exponential mechanism** — which makes the *choice
   itself* private, not just the measurements.
4. **Measure the chosen two-way marginals** under Gaussian noise. A tree over
   $d$ columns has exactly $d - 1$ edges, so this is $d - 1$ measurements
   rather than $\binom{d}{2}$.
5. **Reconcile.** The noisy measurements contradict each other — one marginal's
   implied column totals won't match another's. Private-PGM fits a single
   tree-structured graphical model that best explains all of them at once.
6. **Sample** ancestrally down the tree, then map bins back to values.

Step 5 touches nothing but already-private numbers, so by the post-processing
property it costs nothing. That's the third property from section 5 doing real
work.

### Why a tree?

Of all the choices in that list, this is the one that makes the rest tractable.

Suppose you allowed a general graph of dependencies. Computing the implied
joint distribution then needs approximate inference, so step 5 becomes an
approximation stacked on already-noisy measurements and you lose track of which
errors came from where. A tree has no cycles. Belief propagation on a tree is
exact and finishes in two passes.

So the trade is: give up some dependency structures, and every step after the
measurement is exact and cheap.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — laying out the selected tree"
#| fig-cap: "The dependency tree the exponential mechanism selected. Because selection is private, a different seed gives a different tree — read it as one plausible skeleton, never as discovered structure."
names_ = string.(mst_model.stat_columns)
edges = mst_model.tree_edges
root = mst_model.root

# Depth-first placement: children are spread beneath their parent.
children = Dict{Int,Vector{Int}}()
for (p, c) in edges
    push!(get!(children, p, Int[]), c)
end

order = Int[]
depth = Dict{Int,Int}()
function walk(v, d)
    push!(order, v); depth[v] = d
    for c in get(children, v, Int[]); walk(c, d + 1); end
end
walk(root, 0)

xpos = Dict(v => i for (i, v) in enumerate(order))
maxd = maximum(values(depth))

fig = Figure(size = (1000, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; title = "selected dependency tree (German Credit, ε = 1)",
    xticksvisible = false, xticklabelsvisible = false,
    yticksvisible = false, yticklabelsvisible = false,
    ygridvisible = false, xgridvisible = false,
    leftspinevisible = false, bottomspinevisible = false)
for (p, c) in edges
    lines!(ax, [xpos[p], xpos[c]], [-depth[p], -depth[c]];
           color = (MUTED, 0.8), linewidth = 1.4)
end
for v in order
    scatter!(ax, [xpos[v]], [-depth[v]];
             color = v == root ? SYNTH : REAL, markersize = 13)
    text!(ax, xpos[v], -depth[v] - 0.16; text = names_[v],
          align = (:center, :top), fontsize = 8,
          rotation = π/6, color = :black)
end
ylims!(ax, -maxd - 1.2, 0.6)
xlims!(ax, 0, length(order) + 1)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
@printf("%d columns, %d edges measured — instead of %d possible pairs.\n",
        length(names_), length(edges), binomial(length(names_), 2))
```

That ratio is the argument for the method. Measuring every pair would split the
same budget more than four times as many ways, and every measurement would come
back correspondingly noisier.

### Where MST is strong, and where it is not

Two private engines, two datasets of opposite shape, the same budget each.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The same two engines on two shapes of data, both at ε = 1. Each is better at exactly what the other is not."
function fid(gen, df, seed; hints = ColumnHint[])
    m = fit(gen, df; hints = hints, rng = MersenneTwister(seed))
    fidelity_score(df, sample(m, nrow(df); rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 1))).aggregate
end

b1 = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0)
results = DataFrame(
    dataset = ["German Credit (14 categorical)", "Wine (11 continuous)"],
    MST     = [fid(MSTGenerator(privacy = b1), german, 62; hints = credit_hint),
               fid(MSTGenerator(privacy = b1), wine, 64)],
    DPCopula = [fid(DPCopulaGenerator(privacy = b1), german, 63; hints = credit_hint),
                fid(DPCopulaGenerator(privacy = b1), wine, 65)],
)
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Lower is better. The ordering reverses between the two datasets."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "fidelity distance (lower is better)",
    xticks = (1:2, results.dataset), title = "matching the engine to the shape")
barplot!(ax, [0.82, 1.82], results.MST; width = 0.34, color = (REAL, 0.85),
         label = "MSTGenerator")
barplot!(ax, [1.18, 2.18], results.DPCopula; width = 0.34, color = (SYNTH, 0.85),
         label = "DPCopulaGenerator")
axislegend(ax; position = :lt, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

This is the clearest engine-selection result here, and the one that holds up
under testing. On discrete data MST wins. On continuous data the DP copula
wins. The margin is large both ways.

The reason is symmetric. Chopping eleven continuous measurements into bins
throws away most of what made them informative. Summarising nine unordered
categories with a covariance matrix throws away the same thing from the other
direction.

# 8. Diffusion

Every method so far assumes something about the shape of the dependence. The
copula assumes it's pairwise. MST assumes it factors along a tree. A diffusion
model assumes almost nothing and learns the distribution instead, which it pays
for in data and compute.

The idea is strange: destroy the data gradually, learn to undo one step of the
destruction, then start from pure noise and undo your way back to a sample.

It isn't obvious this should work at all, so take it slowly.

### The forward process

Destroying the data is the easy half. Add a little Gaussian noise at each of
$T$ steps. Because Gaussians compose, you never have to walk the steps one at a
time — writing $\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s\le t}(1 - \beta_s)$, you can jump
straight to step $t$:

$$
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I}\bigr).
$$

So $\bar\alpha_t$ is the whole schedule: the fraction of the original signal
still standing at step $t$.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "A real column dissolving. By t = 100 nothing of the original distribution is left — which is the point, because that is where sampling starts."
const Ext = Base.get_extension(DataMimic, :DataMimicLuxExt)
T = 100
betas_cos, _ = Ext._cosine_schedule(T)
sched = Ext._schedule_constants(betas_cos)

x0 = Float32.((adult.age .- mean(adult.age)) ./ std(adult.age))[1:6000]
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 240))
for (j, t) in enumerate([1, 25, 60, 100])
    ab = sched.alphas_cumprod[t]
    xt = sqrt(ab) .* x0 .+ sqrt(1 - ab) .* randn(MersenneTwister(t), Float32, length(x0))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t    ᾱ = $(round(ab; digits = 3))",
        yticksvisible = false, yticklabelsvisible = false, ygridvisible = false)
    hist!(ax, xt; bins = 60, color = (j == 1 ? REAL : FOCUS, 0.8), strokewidth = 0)
    xlims!(ax, -4, 4)
end
fig
```

How fast the signal dissolves is a choice, and the two obvious schedules behave
very differently:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The cosine schedule destroys signal gradually. The linear one collapses it early and then spends most of its steps on noise that is already noise."
betas_lin = collect(range(1e-4, 0.02; length = T))
ac_lin = cumprod(1 .- betas_lin)

fig = Figure(size = (900, 320))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "timestep t", ylabel = "ᾱₜ (signal retained)",
    title = "how much of x₀ survives")
lines!(ax, 1:T, sched.alphas_cumprod; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2.5,
       label = "cosine (used)")
lines!(ax, 1:T, ac_lin; color = MUTED, linewidth = 2.5, linestyle = :dash,
       label = "linear")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

### Two processes at once

Now a problem. Gaussian noise makes no sense for a categorical column: there is
nothing halfway between "married" and "divorced" to drift through. Adding 0.3
to a marital status means nothing.

TabDDPM's answer is a second diffusion process running alongside the first, on
the same timestep. Instead of drifting toward a Gaussian, each one-hot vector
melts toward the uniform distribution over its levels:

$$
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathrm{Cat}\bigl(x_t;\ (1-\beta_t)\,x_{t-1} + \beta_t/K\bigr).
$$

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Categorical diffusion: a one-hot vector melting toward uniform over its five levels. The reverse process learns to sharpen it back."
K = 5
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 220))
for (j, t) in enumerate([1, 30, 65, 100])
    ab = Float64(sched.alphas_cumprod[t])
    p = fill((1 - ab) / K, K); p[2] += ab      # level 2 was the true one
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t",
        xticks = (1:K, ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]),
        ylabel = j == 1 ? "probability" : "", ygridvisible = true)
    barplot!(ax, 1:K, p; color = [i == 2 ? FOCUS : MUTED for i in 1:K])
    ylims!(ax, 0, 1.05)
end
fig
```

Carrying this in log space isn't an optimisation, it's a requirement.
Probabilities for a 42-level column at $t = 100$ underflow `Float32` if you
hold them directly.

### What the network learns

The training loop, in one sentence: pick a random $t$ for each row, noise the
row up to step $t$, and ask the network to name the noise that was added.
Squared error scores the numeric half; a KL divergence against the true
posterior scores the categorical half.

Once the network can undo one step, sampling is running the whole thing
backwards, one step at a time, from pure noise.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — this is the one slow cell in the document"
adult_sub = adult[1:20_000, [:age, :workclass, :education, :marital_status,
                             :occupation, :hours_per_week, :sex, :income]]

diff_t0 = time()
diff_model = fit(DiffusionGenerator(epochs = 150, batch_size = 4096,
                                    d_layers = [256, 512, 512, 256],
                                    num_timesteps = 100, target = :income),
                 adult_sub; rng = MersenneTwister(70))
diff_secs = time() - diff_t0
diff_syn = sample(diff_model, nrow(adult_sub); rng = MersenneTwister(71))

cop_m = fit(CopulaGenerator(), adult_sub; rng = MersenneTwister(72))
cop_s = sample(cop_m, nrow(adult_sub); rng = MersenneTwister(73))

DataFrame(engine = ["CopulaGenerator", "DiffusionGenerator (150 epochs)"],
          fidelity = [fidelity_score(adult_sub, cop_s).aggregate,
                      fidelity_score(adult_sub, diff_syn).aggregate],
          fit_seconds = [NaN, diff_secs])
```

The copula wins comfortably, and that's not a verdict on diffusion. A hundred
and fifty epochs over twenty thousand rows at batch size 4096 is roughly seven
hundred optimizer steps. The TabDDPM paper uses several thousand, on a network
about four times wider. This document trains a small model for one reason: the
page has to render in a reasonable time.

How it fails is instructive, though, and it shows up in the numeric columns:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
DataFrame(column = [:age, :hours_per_week],
          real_sd  = [std(adult_sub.age), std(adult_sub.hours_per_week)],
          synth_sd = [std(diff_syn.age),  std(diff_syn.hours_per_week)])
```

The cause is specific. The reverse process divides by $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$,
which reaches the order of $10^3$ at the noisiest steps of a 100-step cosine
schedule. Any error in the predicted noise comes back out multiplied by that,
so a half-trained model gives you numeric columns that are far too spread out.
Train it properly and this closes. The mechanism is what to take away, not the
number.

### Making it private: ghost clipping

To put a privacy budget on a neural network you use DP-SGD, which clips each
example's gradient to a fixed norm before adding noise. That per-example
clipping is what bounds one person's influence; you can't bound it from the
averaged gradient, because the averaging has already happened.

Which looks like it needs a separate backward pass per example. At batch size
4096, that would be hopeless.

It doesn't. For a dense layer with inputs $a$ and output-gradients $g$, example
$i$'s weight gradient is an outer product $g_i a_i^\top$, and the norm of an
outer product factorises:

$$
\bigl\|\partial L_i/\partial W\bigr\|_F \;=\; \|g_i\|\,\|a_i\| .
$$

Two vector norms, both already computed. Sum them across layers and you have
every example's gradient norm, and so its clip factor, without ever forming a
per-example gradient. Applying the clipped sum costs two more matrix
multiplications. Two batched passes replace $B$ unbatched ones.

This is **ghost clipping**, and it's an exact identity, not an approximation:
nothing is traded away for the speed. In this package it took DP-SGD from 73.2
seconds per epoch to 0.42 on the same configuration, and the test suite pins
the two routes to agreement within floating-point rounding.

# 9. Evaluation

Three families of metric, asking three different questions:

- **Fidelity** — do the distributions match?
- **Utility** — does a model trained on this work on real data?
- **Privacy** — how close does it sit to real records?

The interesting cases are the ones where they disagree.

### Why fidelity alone is not enough

Start with a trap. It explains the shape of everything else.

Here is a deliberately broken generator: take the real table and shuffle every
column independently. Every column's marginal is now perfect — not close to the
real one, but the real one — and every relationship between columns is
destroyed.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
shuffled = DataFrame()
for (i, c) in enumerate(names(adult_sub))
    shuffled[!, c] = shuffle(MersenneTwister(80 + i), adult_sub[!, c])
end

f_shuf, f_cop = fidelity_score(adult_sub, shuffled), fidelity_score(adult_sub, cop_s)

DataFrame(
    generator = ["column-shuffled (deliberately broken)", "CopulaGenerator"],
    per_column = [mean(values(f_shuf.column_scores)),
                  mean(values(f_cop.column_scores))],
    correlation = [f_shuf.correlation_score, f_cop.correlation_score],
    aggregate = [f_shuf.aggregate, f_cop.aggregate],
    pairwise_error = [pairwise_marginal_error(adult_sub, shuffled).mean,
                      pairwise_marginal_error(adult_sub, cop_s).mean],
    tstr = [utility_tstr(adult_sub, shuffled, :income;
                         rng = MersenneTwister(81)).ratio,
            utility_tstr(adult_sub, cop_s, :income;
                         rng = MersenneTwister(81)).ratio],
)
```

Read the first two numeric columns against each other. On per-column distance
the broken generator is near-perfect, and any evaluation that stopped there
would have ranked it first.

The correlation term is where it comes apart, and that one term is what drags
its aggregate below the copula's despite those perfect marginals. Both
downstream measures agree: five times the pairwise marginal error, and a
utility ratio around 0.57 against the copula's 1.0.

So the aggregate does catch it, but only because it isn't purely marginal. Any
evaluation built solely on per-column comparisons can be passed by a generator
that has destroyed every relationship in your data. Check something
dependence-aware, and check utility too if you can name a task.

### Fidelity, in detail

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
f = fidelity_score(adult_sub, cop_s)
@printf("aggregate           %.4f   (0 = perfect)\n", f.aggregate)
@printf("correlation term    %.4f\n", f.correlation_score)
@printf("columns compared    %d   excluded %d\n",
        length(f.correlation_columns), length(f.correlation_excluded))
sort(DataFrame(column = collect(keys(f.column_scores)),
               distance = collect(values(f.column_scores))), :distance, rev = true)
```

Every number here is a distance, so lower is better. Numeric columns are scored
with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic — the largest vertical gap between the
two empirical CDFs — and categorical columns with total variation distance.
Both live in $[0, 1]$, which is what makes averaging them together defensible.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The KS statistic is a single number with a picture: the widest vertical gap between two empirical CDFs."
vr = sort(Float64.(adult_sub.age)); vs = sort(Float64.(cop_s.age))
grid = range(minimum(vr), maximum(vr); length = 500)
ecdf(v) = [count(<=(x), v) / length(v) for x in grid]
Fr, Fs = ecdf(vr), ecdf(vs)
k = argmax(abs.(Fr .- Fs))

fig = Figure(size = (760, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "age", ylabel = "F(age)",
    title = @sprintf("KS = %.4f", maximum(abs.(Fr .- Fs))))
lines!(ax, grid, Fr; color = REAL, linewidth = 2.5, label = "real")
lines!(ax, grid, Fs; color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2.5, label = "synthetic")
lines!(ax, [grid[k], grid[k]], [Fr[k], Fs[k]];
       color = FOCUS, linewidth = 3, label = "KS")
scatter!(ax, [grid[k], grid[k]], [Fr[k], Fs[k]]; color = FOCUS, markersize = 8)
axislegend(ax; position = :rb, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

The correlation term uses Spearman rather than Pearson, deliberately. Rank
correlation ignores the marginal shapes, which the per-column terms have
already scored, so the two halves of the aggregate measure different things
instead of counting the same thing twice.

### Utility

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
u = utility_tstr(adult_sub, cop_s, :income; rng = MersenneTwister(82))
DataFrame(task = [string(u.task)], f1_from_synthetic = [u.synth_score],
          f1_from_real = [u.real_score], ratio = [u.ratio])
```

Train on synthetic, test on real. Gradient-boosted trees are fitted twice, once
on synthetic data and once on real, then both are scored against the same
held-out real data. The ratio is the number that matters, and it's the most
direct evidence that a synthetic table is fit for anything.

One caution, which comes up again later: ratios a little above 1 are common and
don't mean synthetic beats real. Both scores are noisy, and a ratio of two
noisy things is noisier.

### Privacy

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Distance to the closest real record. The degenerate case on the right is what memorisation looks like."
d_syn  = privacy_dcr(adult_sub[1:3000, :], cop_s[1:3000, :])
d_copy = privacy_dcr(adult_sub[1:3000, :], adult_sub[1:3000, :])

@printf("synthetic      median DCR %.4f, exact matches %d\n",
        d_syn.median, d_syn.exact_matches)
@printf("real vs itself median DCR %.4f, exact matches %d\n",
        d_copy.median, d_copy.exact_matches)

fig = Figure(size = (760, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "distance to closest real record",
    ylabel = "density", title = "DCR distribution")
hist!(ax, d_syn.dcr; bins = 50, normalization = :pdf,
      color = (SYNTH, 0.75), strokewidth = 0)
vlines!(ax, [d_syn.median]; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax, d_syn.median, 0.0; text = "  median", align = (:left, :bottom),
      fontsize = 10, color = FOCUS)
fig
```

`exact_matches` should be zero. The second line is the degenerate case for
comparison: score a table against itself and every distance is zero, every row
an exact match. That's what a generator that memorised its input would look
like.

Treat DCR as a smoke alarm, not a guarantee. Section 4 showed the limit
concretely — that copula had no exact matches at all and still leaked
membership at AUC 0.72. A clean DCR is no substitute for a privacy budget.

# 10. How these break

Everything below is a failure mode that actually happens. Each one was found by
running the code, not by reading it.

### An undertrained diffusion model over-disperses

We met this in section 8. The symptom is distinctive, so here it is again: the
reverse process divides by $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, of order $10^3$ at the
noisiest steps, so any error in the predicted noise comes back out multiplied
by the same factor. Numeric columns come out far too wide.

If your synthetic numeric columns have two or three times the standard
deviation of the real ones, the model is undertrained. It isn't a
hyperparameter to tune away. It's telling you to train longer.

### Rejection sampling is not distribution-preserving

When the reverse process overflows, the offending rows are thrown away and
redrawn. That sounds harmless. It isn't.

Keep only the rows that come back finite and you're no longer sampling from
your distribution — you're sampling from it conditioned on finiteness. And
whether a row diverges is not independent of what's in it. For a
class-conditional model it correlates with the label, because the label is one
of the denoiser's inputs. On an undertrained Adult model this turned a 76/24
income split into 100% a single class, in a table that showed no other sign of
trouble.

So DataMimic tracks the discard rate and refuses rather than handing back a
biased sample:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — deliberately undertraining to trip the guard"
tiny = adult[1:4000, [:age, :hours_per_week, :workclass, :education, :income]]
result = try
    m = fit(DiffusionGenerator(epochs = 2, batch_size = 512,
                               d_layers = [32, 32], num_timesteps = 100,
                               target = :income, lr = 5e-3),
            tiny; rng = MersenneTwister(90))
    s = sample(m, 2000; rng = MersenneTwister(91))
    income_split = [count(==(l), s.income) / nrow(s)
                    for l in sort(unique(tiny.income))]
    "sampled — income split $(round.(income_split; digits = 3))"
catch e
    "refused — " * first(split(sprint(showerror, e), '\n'))
end
println(result)
println("real split: ",
        round.([count(==(l), tiny.income) / nrow(tiny)
                for l in sort(unique(tiny.income))]; digits = 3))
```

Whether that cell sampled or refused depends on how badly this particular tiny
model diverged. Either way the point holds: you get a usable sample or you get
an error. You never get a skewed table that looks fine.

### Seed variance can exceed the difference you are measuring

At tight privacy budgets, the same engine on the same data gives visibly
different answers run to run.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Ten fits of the same engine on the same data, differing only in seed. Each dot is one run; the bar is the mean."
function seed_spread(eps, seeds)
    [begin
        m = fit(MSTGenerator(ε = eps), german; hints = credit_hint,
                rng = MersenneTwister(s))
        fidelity_score(german, sample(m, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(s + 1))).aggregate
     end for s in seeds]
end

seeds = 100:109
lo, hi = seed_spread(0.5, seeds), seed_spread(4.0, seeds)

fig = Figure(size = (760, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "fidelity distance", xticks = (1:2, ["ε = 0.5", "ε = 4.0"]),
    title = "ten seeds, identical settings")
for (x, vals, col) in ((1, lo, SYNTH), (2, hi, REAL))
    scatter!(ax, fill(x, length(vals)) .+ 0.06 .* randn(MersenneTwister(1), length(vals)),
             vals; color = (col, 0.8), markersize = 11)
    lines!(ax, [x - 0.2, x + 0.2], fill(mean(vals), 2); color = col, linewidth = 3)
end
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
@printf("ε = 0.5: mean %.4f, sd %.4f\n", mean(lo), std(lo))
@printf("ε = 4.0: mean %.4f, sd %.4f\n", mean(hi), std(hi))
@printf("\nFor scale, the MST/DPCopula gap on this dataset in section 7 was %.4f.\n",
        abs(results.MST[1] - results.DPCopula[1]))
```

The spread is wider at the tighter budget, as you'd expect — more noise is
going in. But the number to hold onto is the last line. One standard deviation
of seed-to-seed variation is a large fraction of the engine-to-engine
differences you are usually trying to detect.

That's why `compare` repeats every engine across several seeds and warns you
below three. Compare two private engines on one seed each and you're measuring
noise as much as method.

### Numerical failures hide in log space

The categorical machinery runs in log space, and log-space code has an
unpleasant habit: when it fails it doesn't give you a slightly wrong number, it
gives you `NaN`.

A real one from this package. The per-block log-softmax subtracted a single
global maximum before exponentiating. With raw network logits spanning roughly
±100, a block sitting far below that maximum underflowed to zero across all its
rows. The block sum was 0, `log(0)` was `-Inf`, and the whole loss became
`NaN`. Reproducing it needed several categorical columns and a wide batch at
once, which is why it survived so long. The fix was a per-block maximum.

The lesson: a numerical bug in log space is invisible until it's catastrophic.
If training produces `NaN`, suspect an underflow before the learning rate.

# 11. Choosing an engine, measured

Everything above describes what each engine is for. The harder question is
whether any of that predicts what happens when you run them.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
function bench(df, target; hints = ColumnHint[], n = 4_000, seeds = 3)
    sub = df[1:min(n, nrow(df)), :]
    compare([CopulaGenerator(), CopulaGenerator(:gaussian),
             MSTGenerator(ε = 1.0), DPCopulaGenerator(ε = 1.0)], sub;
            metrics = (fidelity = (r, s) -> fidelity_score(r, s).aggregate,
                       utility  = utility_tstr(target; rng = MersenneTwister(95))),
            n_seeds = seeds, hints = hints,
            rng = MersenneTwister(96))
end

results_all = vcat(
    (d = DataFrame(bench(german, :credit_risk; hints = credit_hint));
     d.dataset .= "German Credit"; d),
    (d = DataFrame(bench(wine, :quality)); d.dataset .= "Wine"; d),
    (d = DataFrame(bench(adult_sub, :income)); d.dataset .= "Adult"; d),
)
select(results_all, :dataset, :generator, :metric, :mean, :sd, :fit_secs)
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Fidelity by engine and dataset (lower is better). The two private engines are paying for a guarantee the two public ones do not provide."
fid_rows = filter(r -> r.metric === :fidelity && r.ok, results_all)
gens = unique(fid_rows.generator)
dsets = unique(fid_rows.dataset)
cols4 = [REAL, "#7FA6C9", FOCUS, SYNTH]

fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "fidelity distance (lower is better)",
    xticks = (1:length(dsets), dsets), title = "same four engines, three datasets")
w = 0.8 / length(gens)
for (gi, g) in enumerate(gens)
    xs, ys, es = Float64[], Float64[], Float64[]
    for (di, d) in enumerate(dsets)
        r = filter(x -> x.generator == g && x.dataset == d, fid_rows)
        isempty(r) && continue
        push!(xs, di + (gi - (length(gens) + 1) / 2) * w)
        push!(ys, r.mean[1]); push!(es, isnan(r.sd[1]) ? 0.0 : r.sd[1])
    end
    barplot!(ax, xs, ys; width = w * 0.88, color = (cols4[gi], 0.9), label = g)
    errorbars!(ax, xs, ys, es; color = :black, whiskerwidth = 6)
end
axislegend(ax; position = :lt, labelsize = 9)
fig
```

### What this actually shows

**The public copula wins on fidelity everywhere, and that is not a finding
about algorithm quality.** `CopulaGenerator` isn't solving the same problem as
`MSTGenerator`; it offers no privacy guarantee at all. Comparing them on
fidelity measures the price of privacy. Read the chart that way and the gap
becomes informative: it's what a formal guarantee costs on your data.

**Among engines solving the same problem, shape predicts the winner.** Section
7 ran that comparison properly. At the same ε, MST wins on the categorical
dataset and the DP copula wins on the continuous one, both by a clear margin.
It's the one selection rule here that survived testing.

**The `:beta` / `:gaussian` split flips with the data.** Beta wins on the
categorical-heavy tables, where an arbitrary level ordering creates
non-monotone structure only a nonparametric copula can represent. Gaussian
holds its own on all-continuous Wine, where a single correlation matrix is
close to the right model.

**The error bars are not decoration.** Where they overlap, a difference in
means is evidence of nothing — and a single-seed run would have reported a
confident winner anyway.

### Practical guidance

**Start with `CopulaGenerator()`.** Seconds to fit, strong on mixed types, and
it gives you the baseline everything else has to beat. If it's good enough,
you're done.

**Decide whether you need a guarantee before you start.** Privacy can't be
retrofitted: a non-private model has already seen the data, and no amount of
checking afterwards undoes that. Section 4 is the argument for deciding this
deliberately rather than by eye.

**Match the private engine to the shape of the data.** Discrete → MST.
Continuous → DP copula. The one shape-based rule the measurements support.

**Give every engine a fair configuration.** A diffusion model at a small epoch
count measures your patience, not the method.

**Use at least three seeds**, and read the spread before the mean.

**Check what column detection decided.** It's a heuristic with a silent failure
mode, and a dropped column is easy to miss.
